Inside Trail of Cthulhu 2E: Kenneth Hite on fixing cosmic madness, resisting rules churn, and occult Edinburgh

September 8, 2026 by Andrew Girdwood

Links may earn commission Google News Follow
2 Comments

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 9:11
Instaread

When Kenneth Hite sat down at Tabletop Scotland to discuss the upcoming Trail of Cthulhu 2nd Edition, the conversation quickly stripped away the conventional nostrums of modern tabletop publishing. Pelgrane Press is not overhauling Robin D. Laws‘ foundational investigative engine to chase trends in game mechanics, nor is it forcing keepers to rebuy two decades of shelf stock. Instead, 2E sharpens the system where it actually matters: dismantling the legacy baggage of twentieth-century psychiatric charts, letting tables calibrate the friction of occult rituals, and anchoring cosmic dread in the overwhelming burden of information.

From the mechanics of psychological damage to constructing an occult sandbox across the volcanic geography of Edinburgh, Hite delivered an unvarnished masterclass in practical horror design.

Dismantling the Psychiatric Hit Location Table

For over forty years, investigative horror roleplaying games have leaned heavily on Sandy Petersen’s 1981 masterwork, Call of Cthulhu. Yet that original design model carried an unintentional side effect: madness was treated as an external physical injury. Characters suffered stability damage, rolled on clinical phobia tables, and walked away with textbook DSM diagnoses.

In Trail of Cthulhu 2E, co-designer Gareth Hanrahan dismantled this outside-in framework entirely. Madness is no longer an arbitrary checklist of clinical disorders; it is an internal revelation of cosmic truth.

Back in 1981, when Sandy created the greatest roleplaying game ever in Call of Cthulhu, the methodology was very outside-in: you roll on your phobia table, check whether you have schizophrenia or something else, essentially treating the DSM-IV as a hit location chart. That’s not how a lot of people want to play or treat madness now. In fairness, it’s not how Lovecraft treated it either. For Lovecraft, madness always comes from the inside out. It’s a truth about the cosmos that human minds cannot comprehend, which presents outwardly as insanity. Gareth Hanrahan made that explicit: instead of rolling on a psychiatric chart, the mechanics ask, What is the revelation you have experienced? You centre your roleplaying around that truth. If an alienist in an asylum says you have dementia praecox, that’s irrelevant. You possess the correct understanding of humanity’s place in the universe. You cannot medicalise that.”

By rooting psychological decay in specific revelations rather than medical tropes, 2E protects party cohesion while intensifying cosmic dread. Investigators do not become cartoonish liabilities; they become burdened prophets whose view of consensus reality has permanently fractured.

The Myth of Game Design Teleology

With Robin D. Laws introducing streamlined mechanics like QuickShock GUMSHOE in The Yellow King RPG, some anticipated a radical overhaul for Trail. Hite firmly rejected the idea that game mechanics progress along an inevitable teleological climb where newer automatically equals better.

I don’t believe in the teleology of game design. Mechanics don’t evolve along an inevitable upward line; new mechanics are like new golf clubs, not newly discovered laws of physics. The greatest roleplaying game ever was designed in 1981, and we’re still trying to get back to that standard in many ways. Gar and I agreed that first edition Trail was not broken. The second edition simply catches up with how people actually run the game at the table, rather than bolting on action points or arbitrary changes for the sake of novelty. Sticking with flagship GUMSHOE preserves compatibility with campaigns like Eternal Lies. If we were motivated by crass commercialism, we would have changed everything just to force people to repurchase the entire library.”

That pragmatic stance extends to how 2E incorporates occult magic directly into the core book from Rough Magicks. Magic in GUMSHOE is an aesthetic dial rather than an ironclad tactical subsystem. In high-ceremonial campaigns like Steve Dempsey’s Fearful Symmetries, ritual work serves as an active, daily engine to awaken William Blake’s Albion. In a stark purist scenario, casting an occult rite represents an irreversible, ruinous tear through the fabric of reality. Rather than burdening the table with complex casting steps, the engine relies on Stability pools and narrative stakes, leaving pacing firmly in the keeper’s hands.

Cosmic Entities vs. Terrestrial Monsters

A perennial trap of horror tabletop design is giving numbers to entities that defy comprehension. Hite’s boundary is strict: cosmic deities require narrative stakes, while biological monstrosities require tangible vulnerabilities.

In the original zeroth draft of Call of Cthulhu, Sandy Petersen gave Cthulhu no combat stat block whatsoever. His sole mechanic was simple: an investigator loses sanity on sight, and the entity consumes 1d6 characters every combat round. You can steer an ironclad steamship into Cthulhu, but you do not track damage against a pool of hit points. That divide remains intact in 2E.

Conversely, physical horrors operate within tangible natural laws. Pickman emptied a six-shooter into his basement for practical reasons; Deep Ones bleed, and Ghouls succumb to gunfire. But familiarity breeds contempt. Drawing on the approach behind Hideous Creatures, Hite stressed that being a purist Lovecraftian requires constant reinvention:

Lovecraft invented his pantheon because classic gothic monsters – vampires, ghosts, werewolves – had grown stale. A century later, Deep Ones and Mi-Go have suffered the exact same fate. To be a true purist Lovecraftian, you actually have to mutate Lovecraft’s creations so players face genuine cosmic dread rather than catalogued monster manual entries.”

This design philosophy underpins the upcoming 2E bestiary, Outside Entities. Rather than reskinning conventional monsters, the book mines obscure weird fiction for horrors with distinct operational vectors. Colin Wilson‘s Lloigor feature psychological oppression and energy manipulation rather than being reduced to mere invisible reptiles. Similarly, Wilson’s Nioth-Korghai (the space vampires) serve a unique terror role: unlike the clean mental displacement of the Great Race of Yith, a victim of the Nioth-Korghai remains conscious inside their own flesh, fully aware while their body is puppeted against their will.

Edinburgh as an Occult Engine: Pict-Punk vs. Steampunk

When asked how he would construct a GUMSHOE sandbox anchored in Scotland, Hite seized upon Edinburgh’s unique geographical and historical density. For an urban area of its footprint, the Scottish capital functions as an outsized historical generator:

  • Prehistoric Strata: The Roman Empire reached the volcanic crags and stopped, leaving an ancient Pictish bedrock steeped in Robert E. Howard grit.
  • Geomantic Geometry: Arthur’s Seat anchors local ley lines, King Arthur myths, and the fairy lore of the Scottish Lowlands, echoing Robert Kirk’s seventeenth-century treatise The Secret Commonwealth.
  • Urban Duality: The split architectural identity that produced Deacon Brodie, Burke and Hare, and inspired Robert Louis Stevenson’s Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde (transposed to London only as an operational disguise).
  • Enlightenment Rationalism: The intellectual crucible of Adam Smith and David Hume providing a razor-sharp counterweight of high-stakes academic conspiracy.

Hite contrasted this “Pict-punk” traditionalism of Edinburgh directly against Glasgow’s industrial footprint. If Edinburgh represents deep-time gothic occultism, Charles Rennie Mackintosh transformed Glasgow into an uncanny, architectural dreamscape – the industrial, steampunk counterweight to Edinburgh’s stone-bound dread.

The Cell Phone Problem: Information as Terror

With investigatory fail-forward design now widespread across games like Delta Green, GUMSHOE maintains its edge through structural campaign engines. From the improvisational sandbox of The Dracula Dossier to the sprawling operational networks of Night’s Black Agents, the strength lies in how information propels investigators into danger.

Running modern horror in the 2020s without resorting to cheap “no mobile signal” tropes is a challenge Hite tackled head-on. Drawing from his analysis in GURPS Horror 4th Edition, modern connectivity does not eliminate horror – it widens the attack surface.

Carrying an Apollo-era supercomputer in your pocket cuts both ways. If an investigator pulls out a smartphone and discovers Fomalhaut rises at 9:07 PM, that provides immediate actionable lore; it accelerates play rather than breaking it. But the critical detail is transmission: if you ping an orbital satellite to pull down forbidden data, something can travel back down that frequency to locate you. Ubiquitous connectivity simply creates a larger attack surface. Part of the appeal of 1930s Trail is the deliberate escape from the modern infosphere. But in modern horror, terror stems from information overload. As Lovecraft argued, the true horror begins when you finally piece together all the data in front of you.”

What’s Next for Pelgrane Press

Keepers have an expansive pipeline ahead. In addition to the core release of Trail of Cthulhu 2nd Edition, Pelgrane Press is preparing Outside Entities, an exhaustive field guide to unconventional weird-fiction horrors. Following that, Hite and Gareth Hanrahan will turn their focus back to operational espionage horror with Threat Profiles, an expansive adversary sourcebook for Night’s Black Agents detailing both high-value targets to hunt and the monstrous assets hunting you in the dark.
